To gain a deeper understanding of processes beyond the Standard Model, particularly those involving new heavy particles, B meson lifetimes must be precisely known. This study leverages the full dataset from LHCb and the remaining CMS data from the LHC Run 2 to perform an independent analysis of the $B_s^0$ meson lifetime by studying the decay into dimuons. It utilizes two LHCb detection methods and one CMS method, which employs the $B_s^0$ meson's decay time to study $B_s^0$ meson decays and $B_s^0$-$\bar{B_s^0}$ oscillations, primarily focusing on the precise determination of the $B_s^0$ meson lifetime.

This study deals with determining optimal control for a class of second-class Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations associated with G-BSDEs and underlying stochastic systems driven by a type of fractional Brownian motion. It provides conditions under which a solution exists and proves that a controlled differential equation value function does indeed match this solution. For a broader range of unbounded operator bounds, it also identifies the conditions for this approach to yield reliable results. Finally, an iterative algorithm is presented to compute this solution effectively.

Our analysis of dipole anisotropy in cosmic ray directions divides the dipole amplitude into smooth and fluctuating components, with the latter rising with energy, potentially offsetting the anisotropy trend. To examine this hypothesis, we categorized the dipole amplitude by energy and found that the amplitude per logarithmic energy interval increases from 0.003 to 0.012 as energy rises from 0.5 EeV to 100 EeV, with 0.006 at 10 EeV. This research builds on our earlier analyses of quadrupole and monopole fitting, using the same dataset, and suggests that the fluctuation scale length of 5.4 kpc can fit the quadrupole fit, with possible adjustments at higher energies.

A direct correlation has been observed between the centrality of collisions and the
variation of the nuclear modification factor $R_{pP}$, which exhibits a similar
dependence on centrality as seen in heavy ion (Pb-Pb) data. This interconnection
between the centrality of $p$-Pb and the modification factor raises questions
about the extent of nuclear media interaction in $p$-Pb collisions, particularly in
more central collisions where a projectile proton seems to penetrate the target
nucleus. To investigate this, a model incorporating hydrodynamics is applied to
$p$-Pb and Pb-Pb data, allowing for an estimate of the density of collisions in
the direction of beam in central $p$-Pb collisions. This approach offers a
novel method to quantify the extent of nuclear media interaction in $p$-Pb collisions.

In this investigation, differential operators in a commuting momentum space define
noncommutative quantum mechanics, which are classified into four categories based
on their characteristics.  The fourth category of differential operators corresponds
to the standard noncommutative quantum mechanics introduced by Seiberg and Witten.
A transformation operator connects the types I through III noncommutative quantum
mechanics to their respective differential operators. A transformation operator also
relates type III noncommutative quantum mechanics to its unitary equivalent in a
Fourier transformed space.  Additionally, we establish conditions under which a given
set of differential operators belongs to category III noncommutative quantum mechanics.

The NLM Cancer Imaging Database offers free access to a comprehensive collection of color images of digitized cancer and normal human tissue sections. These sections showcase various therapies and procedures, including tumor treatments and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes. Our approach to detecting tumor infiltrating lymphocytes involves a two-step process. Initially, a random forest classifier with 100000 trees is used to assign each cell the likelihood of being a tumor infiltrating lymphocyte. The second stage is an experimental search for the optimal threshold that maximizes the sum of precision and recall values. When evaluated on a test set of 10000 cells, our method achieved a precision-recall score of.79 for the automatic approach. Furthermore, tumor infiltrating lymph cells can be identified with a precision-recall score of.78 using the random forest approach when only labeled data from a small subset of pathologists is available.

A new optical equalization technique, the Joint Decision-Feedback Equalization, is modified to include5-metric sequence loading in its algorithm. This modification results in the proposed algorithm, which avoids unnecessary sequence loading in its metric calculation, improving efficiency. The new algorithm's performance, comparable to the original, is enhanced, especially in scenarios with significant impulse response lengths and frequent burst errors. These conditions are common in optical communications due to frequent MRZ switching. Additionally, a new algorithm with reduced complexity is proposed, which is based on the observation of sequence evaluation during FE operation. This complexity reduction leads to improved performance, especially in scenarios with short channel impulse response lengths, multiple of-FR switching, and frequent burst errors. Complexity reduction results in overall performance gains of up to 3dB in the proposed scenario.

Recently, highly efficient self-attention mechanisms for FAIR sequences have been introduced, specifically the Transformer-For-AI (FAI) architecture. Although effective, the standard neural network architecture design process is time-consuming due to the vast design space. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique called the Transformer-FAI Network (TCN) self-optimization method for dilation rates. Our innovative algorithm allows a TCN to independently find its optimal dilation configuration, eliminating manual adjustment. Experimental results show significant improvements, up to 19% reduced memory usage and 14% faster inference time compared to the best manual designs. Furthermore, our method consistently achieves better results across various encoder-decoder architectures and tasks. Interestingly, TCN with self-optimization yields optimal results for various design scenarios, outperforming other methods. Our work introduces a novel approach to self-optimization, opening up new possibilities for efficient neural network design.

This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the key properties of Zinbiel algebras, specifically focusing on nilpotency, solvability, lower central series, and upper central series. It specifically examines finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras in doing so.

Fluctuations in flow patterns provide a quantitative measure of the quark-gluon plasma's density and temperature variations, which significantly influences the viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, rather than being a primary indicator of initial position fluctuations.

This paper tackles a critical issue in computational correspondences and modal logic translation: computation of first order correspondents and preimages for (D)LE-inductive formulas. We examine how algorithm ALBA from the authors and others can be utilized to compute first order correspondents and preimages, providing special attention to inductive lattice-based modal logic ALNA. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of ALNA in handling complex formulas, potentially simplifying the preimage computation process.

Our work introduces a framework for consistent query answering using a four-valued logic approach. This framework extends traditional methods by incorporating an assignment-based view of database integrity constraints. We demonstrate that our approach yields the same results as existing approaches, but with a more efficient computation of answer sets. Specifically, we show that our method reduces our problem to computing answers under partial information within a database with a finite number of possibilities, which allows for a more practical implementation. This implementation avoids the need for expensive computations associated with traditional four-valued logic approaches, such as constructing product databases. Instead, we focus on a specific system, K34, where false and undefined values have well-defined properties, further simplifying our computations. Our theoretical findings suggest our approach is as effective as existing methods, but with potential computational benefits over traditional four-valued logic approaches.

We introduce a novel dynamic linear statistical model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX). This model is capable of capturing complex patterns in data, including nonlinear behaviors and frequent shifts, using Kalman filtering and smoothing techniques for estimation. To address model complexity and avoid overfitting, we employ hierarchical models and a no-refresh algorithm for inference. Demonstrations on simulated and real-world data confirm the effectiveness of TV-PARX in comparison to existing models. Additionally, the model's flexibility allows it to be applied to various time series that follow a Poisson distribution.

Despite recent breakthroughs in robot learning, there's still a significant gap between the current capabilities of robots and those required in complex hand-coordinated tasks. To bridge this chasm, this research introduces Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel approach that allows a robot to master tasks with limited demonstrations. By learning a single field to map object states to descriptors, a robot can generalize from a single demonstration across diverse objects and shapes. By combining this descriptor with a simple policy network, the robot can execute complex manipulation tasks, such as handling objects of unknown geometry. Evaluations show that this approach successfully enables the learning of tasks from as few as five seconds of data, resulting in successful generalization to new objects.

The Solid Angle Detector (SiD) is one of the three compact compact muon detectors (CDC) planned for construction at the International Linear Collider (ILC) as an option. The SiD Detector features a comprehensive calorimeter system, consisting of highly granular electromagnetic and hadronic components, designed to optimize particle identification, precise jet energy measurement, and accurate missing energy calculation. This paper presents detailed simulations of the SiD Detector's performance, demonstrating its excellent results in photon and electron reconstruction, including low reconstruction biases and sharp resolution that does not deteriorate at higher energy levels. The calculator also shows outstanding jet energy resolution (<1% for 100 GeV NNJ) and accurate missing energy calculation, with negligible bias below 1 GeV.

We analyzed a previously identified galaxy, Tononzintla 2, using the APOGEE-2 survey, which yielded a high-velocity, metal-rich globular cluster located approximately 26.8 kpc from the Galactic Center. The cluster's age is estimated at 10.8 billion years with a minimal age variation of +/- 0.8 billion years. Uniquely, Tononzintla 2 exhibits a pronounced chemical non-homogeneity, characterized by an extensive spread in the abundance of various elements. A possible explanation for this non-homogeneity lies in the high velocity dispersion and radial velocity spread observed within the cluster. To better understand its non-uniform chemical composition, we compared its statistics with those of the Magellanic Stream, which also exhibits significant chemical non-homogeneity. The analysis revealed that the non-uniform distribution of elements in Tononzintla 2 shares a common origin with that in the Magellanic Stream, specifically the mixing of distinct stellar populations resulting from star formation episodes enriched by distinct supernovae remnants. However, the non-uniform chemical composition observed in high-velocity cluster Tononzintla 2 presents a chance discovery, as it deviates significantly from the typical chemical non-homogeneity exhibited by the majority of other high-metallicity Galactic globular clusters.

Researchers who utilize proof repositories such as Archive of Formal Proofs quickly become dependent on other researchers' proofs as they conduct more research themselves. We investigate the structural characteristics of dependency networks in formal proof repositories, specifically examining how the node in-degree scales, we identify that they follow a scale-free distribution with an inferred in-degree scale of 3.2. We also investigate why this scale is not approaching 1 as the repository grows larger. Furthermore, we find that an increase in the total size of the library results in only a minimal rise (with an inferred scale of 0.2) in the node in-degree of new additions to the library. These observations are explained by considering the primary purposes of proof repositories and the characteristics of modular software design.

The possibility of a confinement-critical end point within a first-order phase transition for pure QCD in three dimensions is found not to hold for $N\ge4$ in this study, which determines the critical value of an instanton moduli space coordinate $z_c$ for the $N=4$ case at approximately $|z_c| \sim 0.8$ through strong coupling expansion, exhibiting a value similar to $|z_c| \sim 0.75$ found in the $N=2$ case. The result is corroborated by lattice simulations for the $N=4$ SU(2) case, which show evidence of $z_c$ lying within the range of $[0.6,1.0]$ with a significant confidence level. The article also presents results for $N=6,8$ within the SU(2) family, along with a theoretical estimate for the critical $z_c$ value for SU(3) at approximately $|z_c| \sim 0.75$.

This study delves into the connection between the solution obtained from the TAP free energy formula and the convergence of the approximate message passing algorithm when solving the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization problem, which has a sparse random Weyl matrix. A key aspect of this relationship involves characterizing the free energy per site using two methods: one developed by Tanaka in 2002 using a virtual disorder transformation, and another using the non-rigid TAP approach. It has been proven that the minimum of the TAP free energy corresponds to the square of the optimal distance from site to site, which is reflected in the large system limit of the total concave upper bound of the free density. Furthermore, simulations were conducted to explore how the relation between site-site and TAP densities can be utilized to identify the convergence threshold of the approximate message passing algorithm. A significant outcome of this work is that it confirms the algorithm's performance can be predicted by comparing the site-density with the non-rigid TAP density.

The GSTCs general formulas can be utilized to create advanced metasurfaces through the implementation of appropriate boundary conditions in Maxwell's equations. Furthermore, a concise and visually appealing mathematical expression results from this process. Researchers have already applied GSTCs successfully to various problems, leading to the development of innovative metallic structures with desirable properties. However, although multiple problems involving electric and magnetic sources have been solved, there remains a lack of practical real-world applications. This study explores the possibility of controlling the flow of electricity on adjacent surfaces by utilizing GSTCs and presents a novel GSTC-based method for designing metallic split-ring resonators modified with magnetic defects that address the issue.

In this study, we explore various aspects of the blowing-up technique in the context of orbital linearization. By proving new results and applying existing theorems, we establish conditions for orbital linearization. Specifically, we address a question regarding the coercivity requirement and establish criteria for orbital linearization. We also prove that the blowing-up technique contributes to orbital linearization proofs and investigate the stability of orbits near singular points. A key finding is that not all orbits in a given region are necessarily orbital linearizations. Additionally, we discuss the application of orbital linearization in studying orbital stability.

Building upon the success of neural network approaches in describing many-body wavefunctions for two-dimensional systems, a variant of the neural network method is presented - the extended correlated neural network method. This new variation, which utilizes a neural network architecture called the edge correlated pixel neural network, is specifically designed to model the ground state of the fractional quantum Hall state at the $s=1/5$ filling fraction. The expectations of observables, such as the entanglement entropy, are calculated for a microscopic torus-shaped system with this new model. The results, which indicate the emergence of topological order and statistical anyonic anyon anyon interactions, are derived from the anyon anyon interactions, which are confirmed by comparing with theoretical calculations. Furthermore, the anyon anyon interactions, which are crucial for understanding the anyon anyon interactions, are found to be consistent with the results of the neural network method. The expectations, which are derived from the anyon anyon interactions, are found to be consistent with the results of the neural network method. The expectations, which are derived from the anyon anyon interactions, are found to be consistent with the results of the neural network method.

Recently, a massive structure nearly 1 billion light years across, often called the 'Giant Arc', has been identified in our visible universe using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. To determine if this finding is a statistical anomaly, we employed a comprehensive redshift survey analysis framework on the complete SDSS sample. This involved assessing both the clumpiness of the universe's large-scale structure and the correlation between object pairs at different scales through a power spectrum fit to the survey data. Our study yields a p-value of 0.6% which indicates that the 'Giant Arc' is an unusual occurrence given its extraordinary size. However, there are alternative explanations including the potential influence of matter distribution within our local universe which can affect our observations. Consequently, at present we cannot confidently explain the observed phenomenon.

Researchers agree that unknown solar variability has a significant impact on the determination of the Earth's radiative balance over long periods, which can be partly attributed to uncertainty in solar irradiance measurements. However, the issue might also stem from the influence of atmospheric scattering that modifies the apparent brightness of the Sun, which has not yet been fully addressed. Therefore, a completely independent approach to determining optical depth (OD) for suspended particles is essential. Based on basic geometry, wide-area photometry can be used to calculate OD for particles oriented perpendicularly to the solar rays, which can then be applied to estimate the Sun's true variability by correcting extratospheric solar flux using an empirically determined scaling factor. Studies on multiple years of data from various stations in Florida and California during total solar eclipses demonstrate increased optical depth values when comparing observations to model calculations, confirming the presence of optical scattering that hinders solar variability measurements. Notably, the approach does not rely on precise instrument calibration as long as relative readings are accurate, and the results from various stations match each other very closely, further supporting the finding of optical scattering affecting solar variability measurements.

Estimating the pose of objects within complex environments and unstructured scenes with limited object cues poses a significant challenge. Existing approaches focused on scene-based pose estimation often suffer from inaccurate predictions when scene context is not indicative of the object's actual pose. This work introduces a novel, architecture-independent method, an attention-guided projection grouping module, that effectively isolates relevant 2D projections from complex backgrounds by leveraging a contrastive context abstraction module. By training a context abstractor to minimize confusion, it uses an attention module to differentiate between context-indicative and object-irrelevant regions in order to better estimate object pose. Furthermore, a soft segmentation mask is generated by projecting the context abstractor's output onto a 2D image and training a loss function to minimize it, enabling a guided grouping module to project 2D-relevant data and preserve structure. Our module's effectiveness is demonstrated on various object pose estimation benchmarks, particularly the Kinect-6D, where it outperforms the baseline and state-of-the-art methods.

In this theoretical study, we demonstrate that in peridynamics, any disruption to the symmetry of the range of interactions guaranteed to result in the formation of a PD crack. Furthermore, we propose that existing non-symmetric kernel structures, which are commonly discarded, may provide valuable information about the location and development of fractures within materials.

Recently introduced 'the Toppo' framework expands upon Graphical Lasso by incorporating latent variables to account for unobserved correlations, effectively separating direct influences from data. However, this enhancement comes with substantially higher computational costs, prompting our proposal of 'Toppo-PL' framework which approximates Graphical Lasso using a proximal algorithm while maintaining efficiency and simplicity of implementation. Notably, our method only requires the selection of a single parameter, allowing it to rival the performance of exact solutions from established algorithms like EM-NET and coordinate descent when given sufficient iterations. Moreover, Toppo-PL demonstrates significant advantages in scaling to large datasets, demonstrating remarkable speed and efficiency.

To evaluate combinations of high-performance computing techniques for reducing computational cost and enhancing simulation accuracy of biomolecular systems, we focused on N-alanyl dipeptide as a test case. We examined the effects of using the AMBER03 and CHARMM36 force fields in conjunction with various numerical methods, including standard integration, the Nos\'e-Hoover Langevin Dynamics (NHLD) and the Cubic-Phase Space (CPS) algorithm. Our results showed that the force field had a more significant impact on simulation accuracy than the numerical method. Specifically, we found that both NHLD and CPS produced comparable outcomes to standard integration, with no substantial differences observed in the calculations of the potential of mean force (PMF). Additionally, we discovered that switching from standard integration to NHLD or CPS and employing the shorter time step of these methods reduced the computational cost, making simulations more efficient.

This study explores the dynamics of binary black holes moving through a fluid environment, utilizing a framework that accounts for both relativistic effects and the fluid's resistance and turbulence. It establishes a numerical model to compute their movements within a three-dimensional, time-dependent spatial framework. The simulation reveals that most binary black hole systems experience stable orbits, gradually shrinking until they merge, but certain initial conditions lead to unstable systems, resulting in possible mergers with a third-gravity well, or even the emission of a black hole if it lacks sufficient mass. It also reveals that fluid interactions cause significant modifications to the systems' momentum, potentially resulting in systems gaining extra momentum that puts it on a different orbital path, or systems acquiring extra negative kinetic energy due to an increase in the mass of the surrounding gravity well. The results highlight the complexity of these systems and the need for further research, especially in systems where a binary black hole is moving through a larger black hole.

This research investigates the dynamic behavior of an elastic system situated on a star-shaped metric graph, where the elasticity on the graph's branches varies. We investigate two scenarios: when elasticity is present only at the central vertex and when it is concentrated there with additional dissipation on the outer branches. We've found that in both cases, the system achieves exponential stability, provided the elasticity and dissipation coefficients meet certain criteria. This result extends a previously established theorem by Di Francesco, Tomasi, and Zambelli, demonstrating that elasticity throughout the graph's branches leads to polynomial energy decay, contrary to our system's faster convergence rate. This new finding fills a significant gap in the literature.

Acoustic imaging techniques have been utilized to analyze the characteristics of two common components used in optical bench construction - Stycast 1090SI and PMMA. By examining the thickness, thickness fluctuations, internal defects, and layering within each material, researchers were able to create detailed maps of their acoustic properties. Through measurements of transmission and reflection coefficients, the acoustic attenuation and impedance of both materials were determined, yielding results for Stycast 1090SI of 0.5MRayl acoustic impedance and 1.25MRayl/internal defect layering as well as 1.1MRayl/layering internal defects and 0.25MRayl acoustic attenuation respectively. These results have significant implications for mechanical stacking techniques used in optical tables, suggesting that techniques such as welding or bonding may need to be explored in order to minimize the reflection coefficients generated by the material.

In the study of multilayer networks, the computation of a node's significance is heavily dependent on the inter-layer connections, with various metrics employing different names for similar concepts of network centrality. A critical issue arises in computation, as nodes within different layers are not evenly connected, leading to a discrepancy in the number of available paths available for calculation. A new method is presented that unifies existing measures by forming a multilayer network with equalized connections, effectively solving the problem and enabling a recalculation of the betweenness centrality based on a shortest path algorithm in a multilayer network.

Recent developments in color imaging using structural coloration have been fueled by applications in flexible displays, quantum communication, and biological vision. Although some structural colors respond sensitively to viewing and source angles, new designs are being explored that prioritize view and source independence, albeit often at the expense of reduced saturation or increased complexity. We investigate how these trade-offs play out in real camera imaging, often overlooked but crucial for practical usage. Our research reveals that a widely used measure of color saturation isn't representative of what's actually seen through a lens, as the point-spread function's color dependency distorts the sharpness of captured images. We also find the monochromaticity of certain structural colors, including enhanced versions, exceeds typical human vision saturation, yet their complex spectral profiles result in apparent colors that vary from those perceived by the human eye. We argue this discrepancy highlights the need for new metrics to evaluate structural colors based on their performance in real-world camera imaging applications.

The study presents an explicit solution to the Dirac equation within the R-Minkowski spacetime, a specific type of coordinate system representing a portion of the global Minkowski spacetime. Within this framework, the Hamiltonian is expressed using 'global' Bessel functions, and the R-Minkowski Dirac equation can be solved by leveraging the properties of these functions and their recurrence relations in the context of the R-Minkowski spacetime. Consequently, the R-Minkowski Dirac equation can be viewed as a de Sitter Dirc equation that incorporates an additional mass term. However, this term corresponds to an effective mass in the de Sitter spacetime, characterized by a sum of the original mass and a mass arising from the boundary between the R-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetimes.

We have developed the CausalGraph modeling framework within the R package 'cdt', 
which was constructed to facilitate the estimation of complex causal graphs 
by identifying parent variables for each node based on local criteria. 
This graph structure captures temporal dependencies between nodes through the 
consideration of existing connections. To accomplish this, 'cdt' integrates 
multiple existing R packages, which include algorithms for estimating local causal 
models and time-dependent graphical modeling. Specifically, each node in the 
resulting graph consists of a set of regression models that depict its causal 
relationships with its parent variables. The 'cdt' package was constructed to 
provide a unified and straightforward method for the simultaneous estimation 
of multiple local models, which would otherwise be computationally inefficient 
and prone to convergence issues, along with an intuitive format for the 
interpretation of results. Furthermore, the package was designed to handle 
time-dependent and node-collapsing scenarios, which were frequently observed 
in practical applications. We have also provided an example analysis to 
demonstrate how the package can be utilized to analyze changing causal patterns 
over time within a single dataset, which was performed using data from the 
National Longitudinal Survey of Youth and includes variables related to 
education, employment, and military service.

This research delves into the complexities of a dual-lip seal system, where a confined space lies between two rotating lips. As the lips press together, they generate pressure that influences their interaction. Our aim is to observe the seal's behavior when the outer lip rapidly moves apart from the rotating component. A non-dimensional equation of motion is developed, combined with pressure distribution modeling, to analyze the dynamics at play. Our findings indicate that as impact speed rises, pressure within the cavity drops, triggering the outer lip to oscillate, potentially leading to chattering. A dimensionless parameter is introduced, revealing a critical threshold beyond which unstable behavior is inevitable, providing a predictive guide for seal impact stability.

Building upon the generalized Witten effect, this study utilizes the Witten formula and the Witten identity to establish a fundamental lower bound for the energy of charged quantum gravity states that transform according to a specific spin-1 representation of the SU(2) symmetry. The constraint imposed by the generalized Witten and Witten effects ensures that such states retain a minimum amount of helicity when composed of states with minimal energy from electroweak theory.

Mobile applications play a significant role in users' daily lives, but the vulnerable nature of these applications poses a threat to personal data privacy. To address this issue, after-market modification techniques, such as OctopOS, have been developed to enable user-app privacy protection interactions. Prior studies on modification techniques focused primarily on functional aspects, leaving user-app privacy-protecting interactions insufficiently explored. In response to this gap, this research aims to present a cutting-edge modification technique, OctopOS, which enables users to secure their personal data while using smartphone applications. Specifically, OctopAfter meticulously presenting the features, design, and implementation of OctopOS in detail, this research will discuss the challenges faced with after-market modification techniques and the potential risks associated with after-market modifications that compromise the core functions and security of smartphone operating systems.

We tackle the challenge of online convex optimization with corrupted feedback in a setting where an adversary can manipulate gradient feedback after each round, with the goal of minimizing cumulative regret. This is considered in the full-information setting, with implications for online learning and adaptive control in settings with corrupted feedback, particularly in scenarios where the action space is large or continuous. We analyze the situation where the adversary does not know the loss vectors but rather gains access to the feedback provided to the learner, considering that this scenario commonly arises in reinforcement learning applications. We demonstrate that a simple modification of the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm can achieve a regret of O(d log d + d log log d) even when the adversary does not have direct access to the loss vectors. We also explore the complexity of achieving a better regret than O(d log d) in FPL with corrupted feedback and provide a guided tour of various scenarios where our findings are applicable.

A variant of the famous "quantum paradox" related to the three-player game has been reexamined through a rigorous mathematical lens, focusing on a critical concept - element of agency. By addressing the ambiguity surrounding agency, a clear resolution to the paradox emerges. According to our interpretation, the resolution resides in acknowledging that only one player's actions within the quantum circuit can truly influence the game's outcome, thus effectively playing the game. Consequently, those outside the solution process, such as game observers or classical programmers, cannot claim to have played the game, despite their apparent involvement. This unique perspective on agency is seen as a fresh perspective that could offer valuable insights into the understanding of consciousness.

First principles calculations and experimental evidence from XPS, ARPES, and optical spectroscopy have been used to analyze the electronic structure of cubanite. Initially, a valence model based on ionic building blocks provided a good fit to the valence band but failed to account for key features like the conduction band minimum, empty states around the $\Gamma$ point, and partial occupancy of certain orbital states. A new model that considers covalent interactions within tetrahedra better matches experimental data including core level shifts, energy ranges of specific states, and energy gaps both within and across bands. This model reveals a small indirect band gap in cubanite and establishes the $\mathrm{Cu}~3d$ states as a distinct peak within the gap. It also explains the ease with which electrons can be added to conduction states and predicts that spin and charge ordering in cubanite can be influenced by conduction electron interactions, a concept that may have implications for understanding the mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in the pentlandite family.

By applying linear response theory and master equation approach, we've developed a theoretical framework to analyze the dynamics of a quantum dot interacting with an acoustic cavity under the influence of an external driving laser. Through numerical simulations, we observed that regular fluctuations in the excitation levels of the quantum dot and acoustic cavity can be induced by adjusting the frequency of the driving laser. In addition, the efficiency of quantum state transfer between the two systems can be enhanced through coherently controlled Rabi oscillations, and this efficiency is modifiable by fine-tuning the driving laser's frequency. Our theoretical model provides a detailed description of this process and demonstrates the feasibility of controlling quantum state transfer through quantum dot-acoustic cavity interaction.

A generalized Hamiltonian matrix, representing a herringbone lattice, can be
simplified to a set of decoupled momenta when specific umbra defects are
introduced. Building upon this, we examine the effects of various local
disorder operators applied to a single site within the lattice, and determine the
resulting topological characteristics through the localization of wave functions.
Our study reveals that by adjusting the disorder operators, we can manipulate
the lattice's properties - from achieving Chern numbers of beyond 1 to disrupting
its topological structure. Moreover, we observe that non-trivial edge modes can
be generated via Valley-Cannibalism, where a particular defect operator
consumes one of the lattice's valley degrees of freedom.

This study delves into the catalytic properties of single-photon catalyzed coherent states, specifically examining how these states can be utilized to transform rational functions of the coherent state's amplitude into irrational functions, with rational numbers as byproduct. We demonstrate that BSCSs and PAccs belong to this category, but they differ significantly in their generation processes, particularly in the probability of single-addition catalysis, with BSCSs exhibiting higher probabilities of successful catalysis compared to PAccs. Additionally, we explore the catalytic effects on rational functions in the large-catalyst and small-catalyst regimes, as well as the impact of catalysis on the displaced and amplified parts of the state, which can be critical for applications in quantum communication and metrology.

The Newman-Penrose formalism utilizes an intricate set of complex coefficients derived from the Weyl tensor's expansion using complex null vectors, with significant simplicity and computational advantages, particularly for solving Einstein's field equations. This study delves into the fundamental principles underpinning this formalism, establishing a solid foundation for those seeking a thorough comprehension, as well as the benefits of adopting the Newman-Penre formalism, with an focus on its direct derivation and presentation suitable both as an educational resource and a reference, with an exploration of various approaches to understanding this formalism, including the role of spinors, with the coefficients in terms of spinors provided for completeness, though not strictly necessary for the other goals, with additional context given to the formalism's applications within gravitational waves, black holes and Kerr spacetime.

A new method has been proposed for inferring a polynomial expression that
accounts for variations in capital letters and ignores inter-letter
permutations. Each polynomial represents a polymere, which is composed of
several monomers that may exhibit different variations. This method defines a
mapping from each possible letter sequence to its corresponding simplified
form through a monomial representation, thus treating the polymere as a
sum of its constituent monomers' effects. If the polymere is cyclic, the
associated polynomial will maintain this property due to the inherent
variability in its monomial components. However, additional conditions are
required to ensure the resulting polymere will indeed be cyclic. A
computational algorithm is also provided to calculate the polynomial
representation for a large set of written names, and the algorithm's
performance is demonstrated with several examples, thus offering a novel
mathematical framework for analyzing names despite any linguistic
considerations.

This study explores the feasibility of ventilating multiple patients simultaneously using one machine. Traditional methods require a separate ventilator per patient, but our proposed approach enables ventilating two patients with one machine. While methods for sharing a ventilator have been studied, they typically result in each patient receiving half the required tidal volume. To tackle this limitation, we developed an innovative approach using magnetic couplers and a dual-volume reservoir technique. This method ensures each patient receives their full tidal volume requirement. Through computer simulations and physical experiments using a lung model, we evaluated our approach by measuring air flow rates and volumes, as well as end-expiratory volumes during the ventilatory cycle. If the additional volume generated by the reservoir doesn't significantly deviate from typical adult resting air flow rates, we consider the method successful. Our results show that our system successfully meets these criteria, indicating that patients can be effectively ventilated using this innovative approach.

A widespread and deadly disease, esophageal cancer, sometimes presents with tumors that have a complicated shape and are difficult to identify. Accurate automatic segmentation of magnetic resonance images requires a robust segmentation framework. This paper introduces a modified version of the UNet architecture, called a Dilated Dense Attention UNet, which incorporates sophisticated channel and spatial attention mechanisms to enhance the framework's performance. This modified architecture allows the model to focus on critical regions, effectively suppressing irrelevant information. To address computational constraints, we implemented a set of modules with varying dilation rates, called DenseUnet blocks, which enable efficient information interaction without excessive computation. We evaluated our method on two public datasets, and experiments demonstrate its superiority over competing frameworks in terms of segmentation accuracy, as evidenced by improved Dice Similarity Coefficient and Hausdorff Distance scores. Our code and results are publicly available for further examination.

Formation evaluation using a logging tool is typically done after a log analysis, which takes logs from the surface and processes them off-line. This traditional approach is slow and inefficient, especially for real-time analysis while the logging tool is in operation. To address this issue, a novel method called Latin-simulated uncertainty management (LSUM) has been proposed for stochastic inverse problems. LSUM allows for an iterative inverse operator to be learned through link predictions within a transformed graph structure. Building on this, a new framework called LM-EnRML has been developed, which combines uncertainty modeling using LSUM with a fine-tuned forward model to evaluate formation data in real-time. Unlike conventional evaluation methods, LM-EnRML can provide instant predictions and handle multiple concurrent measurements, resulting in reduced evaluation times. Experimental results show that LM-EnRML achieves high accuracy, matching traditional methods while being highly efficient. It has outperformed existing formation evaluation approaches in terms of speed and can be applied to other inverse problems with efficient forward solutions.

Our research focuses on developing a simple yet impactful method for injecting corpus-level information into named entity recognition systems, based on conditional random fields. While straightforward to implement, our approach yields a notable 2% improvement in overall performance and as much as a 5% boost in certain categories of the MSRA dataset. Furthermore, our technique is particularly beneficial for rare entity types and entities with ambiguous definitions.

We employ the geometric rational bitangent construction from Bost's 1989 master theorem, which involves a quartic curve that has been twisted in a specific way in its tropicalization, to derive the rationality of the bitangent in a way that aligns with the work of Chen and Cheung in 2020.

The proposed paper presents a new algorithm for estimating the number of sources in multiple-source scenarios. This algorithm, which builds on previous research, refines localization estimation by analyzing the correlation between ideal and actual received signal correlations. A theoretical framework for determining the optimal search step size is also developed. Experimentation using real-world data demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness, resulting in a significant reduction in localization error by nearly 20 meters compared to ideal simulations.

Multilingualism is a cornerstone of many societies, offering a rich cultural exchange opportunity. To improve services for a broader audience, next-generation AI applications, such as multilingual question-answering, are essential. In order to achieve this, computational linguistic research must be proven effective, so it can benefit multilingual societies by means of better data resources and analytical methods. This paper's goal is to provide a comprehensive overview of publicly available datasets, designed to evaluate the performance of computational linguistic models on various tasks while supporting multiple languages. To facilitate the development of robust multilingual models, these datasets can be combined with other inputs. Nonetheless, significant challenges remain unresolved, as the current available resources do not support a wide range of languages simultaneously. This limitation hinders model evaluation across many languages at once. To effectively address the need for efficient communication in multilingual societies, new datasets with strong multilingual coverage are essential.

A significant number of existing image captioning tools ignore the crucial fact that primary users - those with visual impairrances - employ a variety of assistive technologies to navigate the world. Building upon prior research into accessible image descriptions, we observe a significant gap in consistent, user-centered guidelines for creating effective descriptions, particularly in relation to the time these descriptions take to listen to. We further identify a limitation in current image captioning research, wherein the focus remains heavily on improving accuracy, rather than efficiency. To address these issues, we propose a framework for evaluating accessible image descriptions through the lens of visually impaired users. Utilizing this framework, we assess open-access datasets, captioning interfaces, and models, finding a striking discrepancy between the time needed for these elements and the time it takes for these users to scan a page. We also evaluate the quality of existing descriptions through practical utility. Moreover, we establish a new benchmark for accessible image retrieval, which现行 standards fail to address in relation to the time these tasks take. Finally, we suggest a set of principles for developing efficient, usable images, which prioritize the needs of users with visual impairrances.

This study investigates local field, spin-orbit, and longitudinal contributions to energy loss functions within TaO nanoparticles, emphasizing their significance for accurate computation. We employ a numerical method based on the pseudopotential approach to model these effects, utilizing the code VNS in our calculations of energy loss function spectra from TaO.

The online dissemination of fake news is largely fueled by the inclination of individuals to engage with provocative content, a characteristic that compels them to traverse their comfort zone. Despite this, we have identified a contrasting mechanism, where the spatial segregation of users in the online environment amplifies the likelihood of sharing incorrect information. This mechanism, known as "The Big Sort," describes how the online coexistence of geographically separated user groups contributes to an increased probability of misinformation dissemination. To demonstrate this, we examined the dynamics of flatland societies that extend from one dimension to three dimensions. In this context, we found that the magnitude of misinformation dissemination is significantly larger in two-dimensional space as compared to one-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces, a phenomenon that violates our initial expectation that a mechanism promoting engagement with diverse perspectives would result in misinformation spreading more rapidly in one-dimensional space than in higher-dimensional spaces. This observation is further complicated by the fact that the spread of accurate information follows the same general pattern observed in fake news. The unique dynamics of two-dimensional space disrupt these comparisons, revealing the intricacies of one dimension's exceptional behavior.

Weakly-supervised learning enables us to derive valuable insights from limited labeled data, making 50 million YouTube videos analyzable for hidden sexual content. By leveraging pre-training on vast datasets and innovative label generation techniques, our model excels even with small amounts of real labels, outperforming existing methods for detecting subtle cues. With just a few hundred labels, our approach matches the performance of models trained on significantly more data, and by leveraging large-scale weak labels combined with small amounts of real labels, we achieve even better results. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in practice, and to encourage further research into detecting another sensitive category, code and measurements will soon be publicly available.

Human instruction learning is a form of teaching where the instructor uses language to guide others. It is a complex communicative concept that encompasses various situations. This study aims to analyze how different factors affect the core meaning of speech used in teaching. We collected a large dataset consisting of over 11k examples from the Interspeech 2021 Online Workshop on Intenterspeech. Participants were asked to teach a target word by demonstrating its pronunciation and giving clues. Our experimental results showed that changes in demonstration type, instructions, subtasks, and errors result in distinct semantic distinctions within speech segments, as confirmed by acoustic manipulations and semantic annotations. We further tested this finding using a T2A task and found that the distinctions are consistent across different factors, providing valuable insight for teaching-related tasks.

Computer-generated tree diagrams are frequently utilized to represent hierarchical structures, for example in web page layouts. This study presents an innovative method for automatically generating ordered trees that adhere to specific degree constraints and subtree paths. The proposed method allows for the explicit specification of outdegrees for each node, as well as the inclusion of constraints related to the degrees, descendants, and distances between nodes and their subtrees. We model this problem as a shortest path finding task in a specially designed tree-structured graph, and resolve it efficiently using the A* algorithm. The paper successfully demonstrates the application of this method to the generation of well-structured family trees and call tree diagrams for expressions expressed in disassembly language.

The functional differential equations known as Euler-Arnold equations hold critical significance in understanding the fastest growth of a vector field on a quantum manifold within the framework of Finselian geometry. In this context, researchers have investigated the existence of solutions to a constrained optimization problem, inspired by the Schrödinger equation, on a Banach manifold representing the Hartree-Fock space of a many-body quantum system. These solutions could potentially serve as a foundational framework for a non-relativistic quantum theory that accounts for both exchange and correlation effects within many-body wave functions. To this end, the study establishes sufficient conditions under which this optimization problem has solution curves that follow the Euler-Arnold equation, ultimately facilitating the derivation of an abstract, operator-valued time-dependent Schrödinger equation as a side benefit.

Using the Euclid mission, a newly sensitive and large-area sky mapping approach allows for the detection of an unknown Earth-sized object's gravity at a distance of 80 Mpc over 90% of the sky. This discovery becomes easier even with less precise data, suitable for the type of satellite Euclid will provide. By leveraging data from multiple external sources, including future galactic and weak-lensing data, such object's position can be accurately pinpointed with precision measurements of a few arc-seconds. Its gravitational influence can then be analyzed with late-type Baader diagrams and potentially identified with existing or future telescopes like JWST, ANU100, and ANU800. If its mass originates from a lost planet near the Milky Way's Galactic Center, its discovery could provide valuable new information about the remaining mass near the Galactic Center, potentially contributing to the weak-lensing data and the location of luminous and dark matter concentrations. Euclid will provide sufficient detail to determine its radial velocity with late spectroscopy, and future radio interferometers like SKA1 will also be capable of finding it through its hydrogen gas with sufficient sensitivity and resolution. Its orbital period around the Milky Way will be detectable and could provide valuable astrophysical information with minimal complications. Additionally, such small objects could also include lost planets near the Milky Way's core, making their detection possible with multiple detection methods. Their discovery could provide valuable new information about the remaining mass near the Galactic Center,

This work explores the challenge of leveraging memory-based techniques to solve the problem of cross-lingual translation, where source languages and target languages are not mutually related.
A unique approach is proposed, in which the memory retrieval component is trained on multi-lingual data but only the translation module operates in a bi-lingual manner.
Initially, we hypothesize that incorporating the cross-lingual memory retrieval module to suggest source-target sentence pairs will enhance the translation output.
A simple model is presented and evaluated on English to German and English to Spanish translation tasks.
This assessment reveals that the proposed approach consistently outperforms traditional bilingual translation memory models, showing significant improvements and offering potential value for low-resource language pairs with scarce parallel data.

The Planck satellite's measurements of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) temperature anisotropies have revealed some unusual patterns, specifically "hot" and "cold" spots that may have implications for theories about the Big Bang's quantum nature and the behavior of primordial inflation. To explore the relationship between these observations and the prediction of "Hawking points" and low-variance circles that stem from the theory of inflation, we created a novel statistical approach called the conditional power spectrum. This conditionally biased metric, which takes into account the influence of prominent features on the CMB map, is tool to analyze how inflation models, characterized by their spectra and non-Gaussianity, affect the probability of finding circles with specific temperature variances and temperatures, as well as the resulting power spectrum conditional on the presence of these features. This approach was applied to real-world data from the Planck satellite to estimate the probability of Hawking points existing, which is found to be consistent with observations but unlikely to occur if the CMB temperature fluctuations are random, which further supports the idea that Hawking points and low-variance circles may have a common origin with other CMB anomalies.

This study shows that the Yamabe flow, used to find constant scalar curvature metrics within a conformal class, has short-term solution for a certain type of initial data that breaks conventional smoothness standards. This finding relies on an analysis of the Yamabe flow's solution within a specific functional framework, that was initially introduced by H. Koch and M. Lohwiler for short-term solutions of the wave equation on certain three-dimensional manifolds.

A new framework for few-shot learning is proposed that tackles the challenge of unreliable label information. This robust framework addresses the issue of outlier samples that significantly deviate from typical task distributions, causing classification errors. By integrating meta-label information from peer tasks, the system identifies and isolates outlier samples, then updates its task representation through an updated meta-task graph. Notably, the framework requires no labeled outlier data and is parameter-free. Furthermore, it achieves outstanding performance across multiple benchmarks, outperforming current FSL methods under challenging conditions.

User preference description has become an essential component in preference-based recommendation systems. Unfortunately, existing methods that incorporate Gated Attention Networks (GAN) to construct preference expressions are limited by their reliance on a single global aspect, which fails to capture the diverse and item-specific preferences users may have within the same aspect. To address this limitation, our work GAN selectively integrates user preference history by activating exclusive gates for both aspect preferences and user aspects, enabling a more precise representation of user preferences. Our method GATE enhances the GAPE module with the constructed aspects, allowing for a more efficient optimization process and reduced computational complexity. Experimental evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of convergence, overhead, and recommendation performance.

Recent studies have revealed that certain convex cones, such as the cut, elliptical, and indefinite cones, offer valuable natural formulations that outperform extended formulations in various optimization problems, including VRP and PDP variants, scheduling, and flow shop problems. This paper explores the possibility of utilizing these cone-based formulations to enhance the understanding and performance of monochromatic scheduling problems, specifically MFSPP and MCFSPP. By analyzing and reducing the IP formulations for these problems, we derive compact formulations that are smaller in dimension than previously reported extended formulations. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that our proposed formulations yield superior solutions with much fewer constraints than their extended counterparts, resulting in significant improvements in solution quality.

Deep learning technology has significantly提升了 the efficiency of medical image analysis, yet its full potential in neuroimaging research is hindered by the limited and annotated datasets available. This study explores the impact of classifying already labeled data with multiple categories. Using the ADNI dataset for Alzheimer's diagnosis from T1-weighted MRI images, various models were assessed to determine their performance when trained on high-quality data but evaluated on lower quality images. This research found that the dataset composition profoundly impacts model evaluation outcomes. Consequently, the results indicate that employing an unreliable dataset for evaluating models developed with precise data can lead to misleading conclusions about the model's capabilities.

We introduce a new framework for network-based optimization problems involving multiple agents, where each agent contributes a convex cost function dependent on its own contribution and those of its neighbors in a network graph. This framework serves as a unifying concept that encompasses various optimization problems, such as diffusion-inspired applications, distributed and networked convex optimizations. Decentralized optimization problems are viewed as a special instance, with each agent solving the problem locally by minimizing its own cost function. We then analyze two dynamic algorithms within this framework: a gradient-based method and a full-scale algorithm with access to exact minimum values. The results of this study provide a general solution converging to a optimal solution, with the convergence rate rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\kappa^2}{\epsilon^2} + \frac{\kappa}{\epsilon}\right)$ and $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\kappa^2}{\epsilon^2}\right)$ respectively, where the parameter $\kappa$ depends on the arrangement of the network graph.

Hybrid memory architectures that integrate RAM and Optane DC PMMs offer substantial cost savings compared to relying solely on RAM, making them appealing for various workloads. One such architecture features wide-area shared memory capabilities similar to RAM, enabled by a distributed optane memory storage architecture, referred to as the NOVA memory hierarchy. Existing research focuses on shared RAM optimizations, but this study investigates the implications of a NOVA-design on the performance of shared applications, even those with heavy disk I/O demands. Although tailored micro-benchmarks show substantial overhead, largely exceeding 500%, existing tests also reveal surprising findings concerning the benefits of a NOVA file system for Optane DC PMMs, especially during small, persistent writes where performance exceeds that of the attached disk. As a result, adopting a NOVA file system on the edge server level actually improves overall application performance.

Andrzej S. Wierwille's passing in 2020 was a significant loss to the research community, particularly for his groundbreaking work on advanced decision-support systems and autonomous vehicles. One of his key contributions was the Development Dynamics framework, a multi-agent decision-making model that effectively simulates complex interactions between humans and automated systems. The underlying theory of this framework is based on an intuitive concept of underlying "motives" driving observable behavior, allowing for a unified analysis of multiple entities' actions. In this article, we present a specific application of the Motivation Dynamics framework to rendezvous scenarios, demonstrating its versatility in modeling various scenarios of coordinated interaction. Through a case study involving human-robot coordination, we illustrate the framework's capacity to model and predict the coordinated behavior of multiple agents.

This study investigates the magnetic properties of the rare-earth calcongs GdxCmxSn3 (with x = 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8) that crystallize in the γ-therminite structure. Using a combination of susceptibility, neutron diffraction, first-principles calculations, and effective Hamiltonian modeling, we analyzed the effect of the 140 nm Cm on the ground state, anisotropy, and magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE). The results from the VSM and SUS measurements aligned with theoretical predictions, enabling a thorough analysis of the compounds' magnetic behavior. The inclusion of a 140 nm Cm atom flips the magnetic moment of Gd from +5.7 µB to -5.7 µB, causing the easy magnetization direction to shift from the (001) plane to the (001) direction as the magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) decreases from 0.45 meV/Ry to 0.17 meV/Ry with increasing Cm content. The largest MAE of 0.45 meV/Ry is observed in the GdxCm0.2Sn3 compound, but the easy magnetization direction is still located in the (001) plane. This paper explores the intricacies of quark-antiquark interactions within QCD, 
which lead to the formation of mesons, and provides insights into their relationships,
both non-perturbative and perturbative in nature. The discussion focuses on heavy
quarks in the limit where the mass is much larger than the QCD scale, allowing for
an expansion in terms of 1/m. In this context, worldsheet classical solutions for heavy
quarks correspond to relativistic bound states, or 'mesons' with negligible momentum,
and these quark-antiquark interactions incorporate both leading and subleading
contributions, mimicking the effects of virtual emissions of gluons with one-loop
accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the virtual gluon propagator for such mesons,
effectively trifurcating into virtual gluons as a result of the non-Abelian properties of
QCD. The subleading energy scales within this system, stemming from the virtual gluon,
can be correlated to the intrinsic gluonic field within the meson, and we contend 
that this connection may be exploitable for determining the gluonic contribution to the
meson's mass through the optical theorem.

Using a method similar to that used for the symmetric group, we extend the standardization approach of Young tableaux to multilinear rational functions by applying the generalized standardization of the symmetric group. We define the exchange laws for the generalized standardization procedure and demonstrate that the GS-coorder law aligns with the Coxeter length and coorder properties of the symmetric group. Furthermore, we establish a reciprocity relation linking the generalized standardization and co-standardization, and find that the GS-coorder law can be characterized by an alternating sum involving the GS-coorder and Coxeter length.

We present the comprehensive theoretical and numerical groundwork required to
investigate the galactic halos surrounding radio galaxy clusters and systems.
The analysis focuses on determining and limiting the key properties of these
halos, including their masses, ages, ionizing photon rates, photon escape
fractions, radiation energies, radiation fluxes, and characteristic radii.
Our framework establishes essential limits and scaling relations for numerous
parameters that define the physical characteristics of galactic halos.
These parameters encompass the mass and composition of the central supermassive
black hole, as well as the shape of the radiation spectrum.
By applying this theoretical model to specific quasars and radio galaxies, we
demonstrate the calculation of several halo-relevant quantities, highlighting
the potential for observing and detecting ionized gas disks around these celestial
bodies.

This theory provides a framework that extends stochastic calculus from Euclidean space to a variety of related mathematical structures, including vector bundles, manifolds, and geometric objects like Supermanifolds and Supermanforms. Key components of this framework, such as the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, the Hille-Yosida theorem, and the associated ultrashort heat semigroup, have been defined within this framework. A particular focus is placed on the relationship between the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator and the Kato square root problem for a perturbed Brascamp-Lieb-Lieb operator.

Quantum mechanics is explored in detail using a unique ensemble of "tightly confined" T centre defects within high-quality silicon carbone crystals.  Researchers have discovered that these T centres exhibit extremely rapid fluctuations in optical properties, driven by shifting positions of nearby free carriers.  By comparing individual T centres to groups, it's evident that those with more stable positions display optical diffusion at a slower rate.  This research also demonstrates that T centres with "overhang" structures, such as nanoscale silicon carbone columns, offer a more viable option for applying quantum physics principles than T centres embedded within the bulk material.  Notably, the researchers have achieved exceptional stability in a T centre embedded within a 2-nanometer wide silicon carbone column, where it maintained consistent behavior even when exposed to various conditions, including various temperatures and even when hit with high-energy electrons.  This breakthrough highlights the immense potential of T centres as a foundation for implementing quantum technologies in silicon carbone.

This paper proposes three different methods, where the last two are combined, all aimed at automating tumor identification and segmentation in medical imaging. Initially, a database of CT scans is reviewed, and the morphological rules are modified based on this analysis. Subsequently, various tumor detection and segmentation algorithms are explored, and the most effective ones are selected for implementation, including the Modified Morphological Rules, a Region Growing Technique, Level Set, and Active Contour Models. To evaluate the algorithm's performance, a randomized sample of 50 images from the publicly available, open-source, tumor-affected Rabbits CT scans from ORSHT dataset were utilized.

In this study, we aim to delve deeper into the degenerate Bernoulli numbers by establishing their generating function, as well as exploring their associated degenerate Bernoulli polynomials' properties. Additionally, the study incorporates a circulant matrix over a Galois field to further analyze the mathematical concepts at play.

To minimize radial velocity instability caused by spectral lines, we examined line list selection strategies. Although optimal line lists can be determined, their effects on reducing radial velocity jitter vary significantly. Instead of optimizing, we adopted a probabilistic approach and compared it to traditional fitting methods. Additionally, we investigated the impact of line list density and individual line weight on reducing radial velocity instability. Our results showed that randomly selected line lists perform similarly to those selected using standard methods. Line lists with more sampled lines exhibit less radial velocity instability, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Moreover, individual line weight has a notable impact on reduction of radial velocity instability. This has implications for automated analysis pipelines that utilize high-resolution spectroscopy.

This research focuses on designing low-power range sectors for wide-area sensor networks that operate on multiple hops. We propose a novel approach called Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS) that organizes nodes into hierarchical clusters using a localized protocol. Each node within the network maintains its own independent sector, which is designed to minimize interference, often referred to as the "hidden terminal" problem. We have developed a mathematical framework to analyze the energy consumption and data transmission costs of HRS, which surprised us by showing that on average, each node only needs to transmit data once per unit, significantly lowering our initial expectations. To validate these findings, we constructed a simulation called Multi-Hop MTSN, which accounts for various real-world factors such as energy consumption patterns, data transmission costs, and network routing. The simulation results highlight the advantages of HRS in terms of its simplicity and robustness, which allow it to effectively manage network performance without the need for complex tuning, even in multi-hop scenarios.

The selection of an object detector is contingent upon the specific application in question. To achieve optimal performance, deep learning-based detectors are often trained for countless cycles, though this process can be computationally expensive, especially when utilizing high-quality detectors like Mask R-CNN, in relation to simpler options like Faster R-CNN. To address these limitations, our research aims to determine the most suitable detector for a given task without incurring unnecessary overhead. MakeChoice, our proposed framework, dynamically evaluates multiple detector options object-by-object, balancing the overhead of different detectors against their performance benefits. MakeChoice is flexible, compatible with any regression method, and can be easily adapted to utilize different detector backbones. Experimental results demonstrate significant overall accuracy improvements of up to 5.7% compared to the conventional use of a single detector option.

This study focuses on a specific type of elliptic system, with the condition that certain components of the system grow faster than others as their variables increase, under a particular growth rate constraint. The novel approach employed in this research requires minimal assumptions regarding the relative growth rates of the growth rate constraints. This approach yields multiple benefits, with certain implications relaxing previous conditions and new conditions being considered. The elliptic system in question possesses localized solutions for a specific range of parameters, with the growth rate constraints being also relaxed.

This study seeks to improve existing bounds related to concentration results by K. L. Jarrow and R. L. Taylor, which apply to standard independent Bernoulli random variables conditioned on the outcome of the sum. Various results related to concentration can then be derived for convex functions, as well as moments of powers and factorials of the sum. Specifically, the paper obtains new bounds for a wide range of applications including Bessel function expansions, hypergeometric distributions, and combinatorial inequalities such as Turan inequalities and combinatorial identities. The derived bounds are particularly valuable in statistical testing, information theory, and combinatorial analysis. The paper also derives an explicit bound for the entropy of such Bernoulli random variables and uses this to obtain a bound for the relative entropy of such Bernoulli random variables, which in turn can be applied to conditional distributions of hypergeometric random variables. The results of this study have implications for concentration of convex functions and polynomials of standard independent Bernoulli random variables conditioned on the outcome of the sum, with particular attention given to applications in combinatorial inequalities and moment bounds. The derived bounds for the entropy and relative entropy can be utilized in combinatorial inequalities such as the derivation of bounds for the entropy and relative entropy of such Bernoulli random variables. The paper also obtains new bounds for the concentration of convex functions and polynomials of standard independent Bernoulli random variables conditioned on the outcome of the sum, which in turn can be utilized

Let $S$ be a smooth scheme of dimension one over a $p$-adic ring $A$. This work compares the torsion versions of crystalline and étale cohomology of $S$ by leveraging Faltings' comparison isomorphism in a geometric setting of dimension one, thus proving a localized form of the Faltings-Verdier-Hodge conjecture. Furthermore, the paper explores connections with quadratic forms over curves and provides an 11-dimensional dimension reduction theorem for quadratic forms over functions fields.

To effectively measure the $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry in the Drell--Lehan effect, we need to consider the impact of finite lepton masses and ensure precision by accounting for momentum cuts, invariant mass, and the dihadron invariant mass. Additionally, our analysis reveals that measuring $\cos\theta_R$ asymmetry is vital for investigating the dihadron fragmentation function (DiFF) through process like $pp \to \ell \+j$ production, particularly in determining the diagonal and off-diagonal DiFF contributions. To achieve this, we examine theoretical dijet cross sections derived from calculations that include color octet contributions, using the Monte Carlo program PyDiHAD, and compare these to predictions based on a diagonal DiFF. We emphasize that more experimental and theoretical research is necessary to address this complex issue.

which leads to a straightforward derivation of the inverse formula. 
We propose that the invariant quantity inherent in Fock's transformation involves 
rotating the five-vectors within the five-dimensional Minkowski space, 
which yields a clear understanding of the inverse transformation. 
Furthermore, we demonstrate that the invariant quantity can be expressed as 
a De Sitter spacetime interval, which appears as a De Sitter 
hypersurface within the five-dimensional Minkowski space. 

The fact that the inverse transformation can be derived from a De Sitter 
invariant quantity suggests a deeper underlying mechanism, which might inform 
future research into quantum gravity within De Sitter spacetime. 
We also establish a direct connection between Fock's invariant and the 
Cremer-Bargmann spinor, which we show can be derived by rotating the 
five-velocity within the five-dimensional Minkowski space. 
As a result, the spinor can be viewed as a tangent space spinor within De Sitter

intervals, we establish that it is equivalent to the squared norm of a 'bispinor', 
which is found to be a Cremer-Bargmann spinor within a rotated frame within the
